newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish GDP booms 7.6 pct in Q1 '97 - institute.
newsitem.headline: Polish GDP booms 7.6 pct in Q1 '97 - institute.

text.p: Poland's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997, against five percent growth in the same quarter of last year, the independent Gdansk Market Economy Institute (IBnGR) said.
In its quartely economic forecast the IBnGR revised up the 1997 GDP forecast to 5.7 percent growth from its previous 5.4 on the back of fast growth in the first months of the year.

"Economic growth was exceptionally fast in the first quarter as the winter was relatively mild, investment remained high and domestic demand was still growing," deputy head of IBnGR Maciej Grabowski told a news conference on Thursday.
The Polish government envisions GDP growth of between five and 5.5 percent in this year's budget.
Grabowski said that according to the GDP model used by the Central Statistical Office (GUS), the Polish economy may have grown as much as eight percent in the first quarter.
GUS is due to release official first quarter data in May.

The IBnGR said Poland's economy, which has been driven by booming domestic demand since the second half of 1996, will slowly cool amid a tight monetary and fiscal policy until a modernised manufactoring sector can again boost exports.
"A smooth transition can be in the works as modernisation and recent (foreign) capital injections in Polish industry should bring results in the mid-term," Grabowski said.

The IBnGR said an official interest rate cut was not expected in the second quarter and that rates should remain high for the rest of the year to stifle quickly growing domestic demand, especially demand for consumer goods.
"There is no need to change interest rates in the near term. The psychological effects from any cut could boost credit, which is not needed," IBnGR analyst Miroslaw Gronicki, also present, said.

The IBnGR said the main problem for the Polish economy this year was the widening trade deficit, which the institute forecast to widen the current account gap to $7.5 billion in 1997 from $1.4 billion last year.

"In 1997 the current account gap will not be neutralised, as it was in past years, by foreign direct investment...and cross-border trade inflows, resulting in a decrease of currency reserves," Gronicki said.
The IBnGR expected official currency reserves, those held by the state, to fall to between $16.2-$16.7 billion by the end of 1997 from $18.3 billion in February.
It said reserves in the whole banking system should fall to between $19.4-$20.0 billion from $21.1 billion in March.
The institute expected average year-on-year inflation to fall to 14.5 percent in the fourth quarter from 17.2 percent over the first three months of 1997.
